hints: Look for what is shared by ALL three tubes. Something is present in the trachea and bronchi but disappears when you get down to the tiny bronchioles.
Think about the mucus escalator. Which lining with tiny hairs plus goblet cells is needed all the way down the airways to trap dust and sweep it upwards?
walkthrough:
**Spot what the question is asking**

Notice the word typically found in the trachea, bronchi AND bronchioles. We need a feature common to all three, not just one or two of them.

Think of the airway getting narrower as you go down.

**Compare support versus lining**

The wall support changes down the tree. Trachea has C-shaped cartilage rings, bronchi have cartilage plates, but bronchioles have no cartilage at all, only smooth muscle.

The lining, however, stays the same. All three are lined by ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.

**Pick the common feature**

Cilia beat in a coordinated wave to move mucus with trapped pathogens and dust up toward the throat. This is essential in all three airways.

Squamous linings are for very thin exchange surfaces, not for these conducting airways.

options.A: Cartilage supports the trachea and bronchi but is absent from bronchioles, so it is not found in all three.
options.B: Ciliated epithelium with mucus-secreting goblet cells lines the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to trap and sweep out debris.
options.C: Squamous epithelium is the very thin lining of the alveoli for gas exchange, not the lining of the conducting airways.
options.D: Squamous endothelium lines blood vessels and capillaries, not the airways of the gas exchange system.
